entries.topic: Puritan and 17th-18th century restorationism; London Society 1809

claims.text: Restorationism is 'the pre-twentieth-century Christian belief that the Jewish people would return' to Palestine; it 'is not synonymous with either premillennialism or dispensationalism' and 'significantly predates Darby's innovations' (Crome).

Thomas Brightman (1562-1607), Puritan commentator and serving Church of England minister, argued in posthumously published commentaries on Daniel, Revelation and the Song of Songs that the Jews would convert and rule from Palestine; his ideas first appeared in print in the United Provinces in 1609.
Brightman and other commentators had suggested 1656 as the date for Jewish restoration.

Henry Finch, lawyer and MP, published The World's Great Restauration, or Calling of the Jews in 1621; James I treated it as a libel; Finch was arrested in April 1621 and released after disavowing passages derogatory to the sovereign; Laud referred to it in a July 1621 sermon and it was suppressed.
Crome: Finch was imprisoned by the Court of High Commission after suggesting kings would lay their crowns before the Jews in Jerusalem.
Increase Mather, The Mystery of Israel's Salvation (1669), expected the Jews to return to Palestine before their conversion; reaffirmed in his 1709 Dissertation.

Cromwell convened the Whitehall conference on readmitting Jews in December 1655; Menasseh ben Israel argued on commercial and prophetic grounds; the conference ended without resolution; in 1656 Cromwell quietly recognized a small Jewish community in London. Jews had been expelled in 1290.

Crome rejects the view that restorationism went into hibernation between the 1650s and the French Revolution; it remained 'an established part of Protestant discourse' (Thomas Newton, John Gill); the American and French revolutions increased prophetic speculation; Richard Brothers in 1795 claimed to be 'king of the Hebrews'.

The London Society for Promoting Christianity amongst the Jews was founded in 1809, initially non-denominational, through the convert Joseph Frey; in 1815 it was reconstituted as an Anglican society, financed by Lewis Way, after running large debts.

Crome: 'the vast majority of restorationists attempted to effect the conversion of Jews to Christianity'; that call 'was often seen by Jews themselves as a form of both personal and corporate attack'.

Lewis (2010), per Sandmel: evangelical philosemitism ('Teaching of Esteem') tied to British self-image as an elect nation and to anti-Catholic identity; Sandmel criticises that the tension with conversion goals is unexplored and Jews are largely absent from the account.

sources.label: Andrew Crome, 'Christian Restorationism Prior to 1900', Critical Dictionary of Apocalyptic and Millenarian Movements, 20 February 2022
David Fox Sandmel, review of Donald M. Lewis, The Origins of Christian Zionism (Cambridge UP, 2010), Studies in Christian-Jewish Relations 6 (2011)

entries.topic: Shaftesbury, Palmerston 1840, the Jerusalem bishopric, Keith and the slogan, Hechler, to 1891

claims.text: Shaftesbury (Lord Ashley) married Lady Emily Cowper on 10 June 1830; she was Palmerston's stepdaughter (and, the article says, likely his natural daughter).

Shaftesbury helped persuade Palmerston to send William Tanner Young to Jerusalem as British vice-consul in 1838; Young arrived in 1839, was a Shaftesbury protégé, from mid-1839 asked Palmerston for British protection for Jews, and became consul 1841-45.

Ashley's January 1839 Quarterly Review article (reviewing Lord Lindsay's Letters) was the first proposal by a major politician to resettle Jews in Palestine and argued the land's economic value to Britain ('Capital and skill are alone required', via Masalha 2014).

In 1840 Ashley persuaded Palmerston to pursue a Jewish protectorate idea; Palmerston had the ambassador suggest it to the sultan without informing the cabinet; the sultan did not view it favourably; Ashley's diary says he was 'forced to argue from worldly reasons' as Palmerston had little interest in prophecy.

Palmerston to Ponsonby, 11 August 1840 (FO 78/390, No. 134): Jews of Europe have 'a strong notion that the Time is approaching when their nation is to return to Palestine'; if they returned 'under the sanction and protection, and at the invitation of the Sultan' they would be 'a check upon any future evil designs of Mehemet Ali or his Successor'; 'It is well known that the Jews of Europe possess great wealth.'

Jerusalem bishopric: proposed by Frederick William IV via Bunsen; Act of 1841 in force 5 October; £30,000 endowment for £1,200 a year; alternate English/Prussian nomination with Canterbury veto; Michael Solomon Alexander, former Plymouth rabbi, convert 1825, LJS missionary and King's College Hebrew professor, consecrated 7 November 1841, in Jerusalem early 1842, died 23 November 1845; successor Samuel Gobat; agreement abolished by Prussia 3 November 1886; opposed by Tractarians, a catalyst of Newman's conversion.
Crome: the bishopric was established through Shaftesbury's work with Bunsen, partly funded by the LJS, seen by restorationists as preparing Jews for conversion, with little practical effect.
Shaftesbury president of the LJS from 1848; helped found the Palestine Exploration Fund (1865); his political influence waned from the mid-1850s.

Lewis (per Sandmel) calls Shaftesbury the 'leading Christian Zionist of the nineteenth century'; his three aims (consul, Anglican church, joint bishopric) achieved by 1849; Lewis traces a line from his advocacy to attitudes that helped produce Balfour 1917.
Earliest wording cited: Methodist Richard Watson (d. 1833), sermon: 'There is a people without a country, and a country without a people.'

Alexander Keith, Church of Scotland, travelled to Palestine in 1839; his 1843 The Land of Israel According to the Covenant with Abraham... called the Jews 'a people without a country' and their land in a great measure 'a country without a people'; the exact formula 'a land without a people and a people without a land' first appeared in an 1844 review of Keith in a Free Church magazine.

Shaftesbury, July 1853 letter (to Aberdeen per Wikipedia; to Palmerston per Muir): Greater Syria 'a country without a nation' needing 'a nation without a country'; diary 1854 similar; 1875 PEF meeting 'a country without a people'.

Zangwill, New Liberal Review, December 1901: 'Palestine is a country without a people; the Jews are a people without a country' - first Zionist use per Muir; c.1904 he said 'Palestine proper has already its inhabitants'.

Muir: in seven major US newspapers through 1948 'Jewish national home' appears 3,000+ times, Zangwill's wording four times (before 1906); she finds no Zionist organisation or leader used it as a slogan and it is absent from Herzl's writings; she reads 'people' as nation.

Contrary readings: Anita Shapira and Boaz Neumann say the phrase was common among early Zionists; Khalidi calls it a 'widely propagated Zionist slogan' expressing a belief Palestine was empty; Said; Masalha; Kramer: 'Palestine contained people, but not a people'.

Hechler (b. Benares 1 Oct 1845, d. London 30 Jan 1931), chaplain to the British embassy in Vienna 1885-1910, wrote The Restoration of the Jews to Palestine (1884), predicting a major event in 1897 or 1898 from a 1,260-year reckoning from Omar's reign; met Herzl 10 March 1896 (Herzl: 'a naive visionary with a collector's enthusiasm'); arranged Herzl's audience with the Grand Duke of Baden 25 April 1896; attended First Zionist Congress 1897; did not hold conversion a precondition of return.
JTA 1931: Hechler introduced Herzl to Wilhelm II and accompanied him when the Kaiser received him in Jerusalem; Herzl's diaries mention him more often than anyone else; chaplain 1885-1910.
Blackstone presented his memorial to President Harrison and Secretary Blaine in March 1891; in 1916 Brandeis called him the 'Father of Zionism' (per Crome).

entries.topic: Audit re-checks for Part Two (21 October 2026)

claims.text: Audit: Muir names the recipient of Shaftesbury's July 1853 letter as 'Foreign Minister George Hamilton Gordon, Lord Palmerston' (George Hamilton Gordon was Aberdeen's name); she dates Hodder's biography 1887; Keith returned to Palestine five years after 1839 with his son George Skene Keith. Muir does not mention Himmelfarb (the Himmelfarb reading is from the Wikipedia article).

Audit: Wikipedia quotes Adam Garfinkle from Jewcentricity (2009): early Zionists who validated the phrase 'did not do so easily or for long'; Neumann cites a book by Ben-Gurion and Ben-Zvi and finds pioneer writings 'full of expressions of Palestine as an empty and desolate land'; Zangwill 1917: 'The country holds 600,000 Arabs'; Said, 'cancel and transcend an actual reality'; Masalha, 'no people worth considering'.

Audit: Hechler was tutor to the children of Frederick I, Grand Duke of Baden, from about 1873; used Philipp zu Eulenburg to approach the Kaiser; wrote 'It is the duty of every Christian to love the Jews'.

Audit: Crome confirms Brightman 'favoured Presbyterian church government'; Cromwell's July 1653 hope that the Barebones Parliament might help 'bring the Jews home'; Menasseh's 'ends of the earth' argument; Mather on the Jews overcoming the Roman Church and Ottoman Empire; Brothers a former naval officer promising restoration by 1798; the London Society 'denied any particular focus upon prophecy'.
